source_text:
Εὔλογόν ἐστιν λοιπὸν ἀνανῆψαι ἡμᾶς, ὡς ἔτι καιρὸν ἔχομεν εἰς θεὸν μετανοεῖν. καλῶς ἔχει, θεὸν καὶ ἐπίσκοπον εἰδέναι. ὁ τιμῶν ἐπίσκοπον ὑπὸ θεοῦ τετίμηται: ὁ λάθρα ἐπισκόπου τι πράσσων τῷ διαβόλῳ λατρεύει.
πάντα οὖν ὑμῖν ἐν χάριτι περισσευέτω: ἄξιοι γάρ ἐστε. κατὰ πάντα με ἀνεπαύσατε, καὶ ὑμᾶς Ἰησοῦς Χριστός. ἀπόντα με καὶ πάροντα ἠγαπήσατε. ἀμοιβὴ ὑμῖν ὁ θεός, δἰ ὃν πάντα ὑπομένοντες αὐτοῦ τεύξεσθε.
thought_title: Honor the bishop; God will repay
orientation: Ignatius is closing his letter to the Smyrnaeans, urging them to use the remaining time for repentance and to honor the bishop, and promising that God will reward their love shown to him.
pass_a_gloss: It is reasonable [for] the rest [of the time] [for] us to come to our senses, since still [we] have opportunity to repent toward God. [It] is good, God and [the] bishop to know. The [one] honoring [the] bishop has been honored by God; the [one] secretly from [the] bishop doing anything to the devil serves. All [things] therefore among you in grace let abound; for worthy you are. In all [things] me you refreshed, and you Jesus Christ [will refresh]. Absent me and present you loved. [The] reward [for] you [is] God, through whom all [things] enduring him you will obtain.

choices.why: The verb means to sober up or regain right judgment; 'come to our senses' keeps the moral awakening sense without importing a modern idiom about alcohol.

choices.english: to know God and the bishop
choices.why: The infinitive εἰδέναι means to know or acknowledge; the pairing of God and bishop is deliberate and should stay close to the Greek word order.
rejected: to recognize God and the bishop
to be acquainted with God and the bishop

choices.english: the one who does anything secretly without the bishop
choices.why: λάθρα with genitive means 'secretly from' or 'without the knowledge of'; 'without the bishop' is the natural English for acting behind the bishop's back.
rejected: the one who acts secretly from the bishop
the one who does anything in secret apart from the bishop

choices.why: ἀμοιβή is recompense or return; making God the reward preserves the striking equation of the sentence.

choices.term: δἰ ὃν πάντα ὑπομένοντες αὐτοῦ τεύξεσθε
choices.english: by enduring all things through him you will obtain him
choices.why: The relative pronoun ὃν refers to God, and the genitive αὐτοῦ is the object of τεύξεσθε; the clause means enduring everything for God's sake leads to obtaining God himself.
rejected: through whom, enduring all things, you will attain him
for whose sake enduring all things you will obtain him

pass_b_english: It is good for us now to come to our senses, while we still have time to repent and turn to God. It is good to know God and the bishop. Whoever honors the bishop has been honored by God. Whoever does anything in secret from the bishop serves the devil.

So let everything abound among you in grace, for you are worthy of it. You have refreshed me in every way, and Jesus Christ will refresh you. You loved me both when I was absent and when I was present. God is your reward: through him, enduring all things, you will obtain him.

problems.quote: by enduring all things through him, you will obtain him
problems.source_quote: δἰ ὃν πάντα ὑπομένοντες αὐτοῦ τεύξεσθε
problems.why: δἰ ὃν = 'for whose sake' or 'because of whom,' not 'through him.' The relative pronoun ὃν refers back to God as the one for whose sake they endure, not the means by which they endure.
problems.fix: for whose sake you endure all things, you will obtain him

problems.why: λαθρα + genitive means 'secretly from/hidden from the bishop,' not 'without the bishop.' The sense is doing things behind the bishop's back, not merely in his absence.
problems.fix: whoever does anything in secret from the bishop serves the devil
problems.ruling: λάθρα means 'secretly/stealthily'; doing something λάθρα ἐπισκόπου is behind the bishop's back, not merely 'without' him.

edits.old: by enduring all things through him, you will obtain him
edits.new: for whose sake you endure all things, you will obtain him

edits.old: whoever does anything secretly without the bishop serves the devil
edits.new: whoever does anything in secret from the bishop serves the devil

problems.quote: for whose sake you endure all things, you will obtain him
problems.source_quote: δἰ ὃν πάντα ὑπομένοντες αὐτοῦ τεύξεσθε
problems.why: δἰ ὃν = 'through whom' (God), not 'for whose sake'; ὑπομένοντες = 'enduring' (present participle), not 'you endure'
problems.fix: through whom, enduring all things, you will obtain him
problems.ruling: δἰ ὃν means 'through whom' (God), not 'for whose sake'; ὑπομένοντες is participle 'enduring', not finite 'you endure'.

edits.old: for whose sake you endure all things, you will obtain him
edits.new: through whom, enduring all things, you will obtain him

last_rejected.quote: through whom, enduring all things, you will obtain him
last_rejected.source_quote: δἰ ὃν πάντα ὑπομένοντες αὐτοῦ τεύξεσθε
last_rejected.why: Greek has 'through whom' (God/Christ) but 'obtain him'—the relative pronoun δἰ ὃν is masculine, referring to God (ὁ θεός), but αὐτοῦ is masculine too. However, 'enduring all things' modifies 'you' (participle), and 'you will obtain him'—but the Greek says αὐτοῦ τεύξεσθε, 'you will obtain him.' The English 'through whom... you will obtain him' is grammatically possible but awkward. More importantly, 'through whom' should likely be 'for whom' or 'on whose account'—διά with accusative can mean 'for the sake of,' 'on account of.' 'Through whom' suggests means, but here it's likely cause/reason: 'for whose sake, enduring all things, you will obtain him.'
last_rejected.fix: for whose sake, as you endure all things, you will obtain him
last_rejected.ruling: διά + acc. regularly means 'through whom'; rendering is within normal range. Claim is a preference, not a meaning change.

polish.changed: Clarified the final sentence so that 'through whom' clearly refers to God, and made the reward statement read naturally in modern English while preserving every claim.

notes.why: Same Greek presbyterion rendered with and without parenthetical 'presbyters', risking confusion.
notes.fix: Use consistent 'council of elders' with note.

notes.quote: council of elders in the place of the council of the apostles
notes.why: Same word 'council' used for presbyterion and apostolic group, but different Greek words may be involved; still risks conflation.
notes.fix: Note Greek terms or use 'college of apostles' if distinct.
